sections.h2: Paying your Ohio County tax bill
sections.html:
Walk-in payments are accepted at the sheriff's tax office, 301 South Main Street, Hartford. If you would rather mail a check, address it to PO Box 186, Hartford, KY 42347. The phone line is 270-298-4444.

Counter hours run 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. on weekdays, with a half day (8 a.m. to noon) on the first and last Saturday of each month. After hours there is a drop box on the door. Mailed checks are honored by postmark, but never mail cash. A card works at the counter, and the sheriff's website has an online payment link. Refund checks, such as those that follow a corrected assessment, go out at the end of each month, and the same phone line handles refund questions.

The sheriff does not set values. For a question about an assessment, an address on the bill or an exemption, call the Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) at 270-298-4433.

sections.h2: What Ohio County looks like for a seller
sections.html:
Land stretches a long way in Ohio County and people are spread thin. Hartford is the seat, Beaver Dam is the biggest town, prices are modest and almost nothing new gets built, so listings are nearly all resales. Population is 23,934 for July 2025, up 0.7 percent from April 2020.

  • Typical value of an owned house: $121,400, with $1,105 in monthly costs for owners who carry a mortgage.
  • Owners live in 77.2 percent of the 9,107 households.
  • Median household income is $57,798.
  • The county has 10,377 housing units and issued just 3 building permits in 2025.
  • Renters pay a median gross of $739 a month.

With so little turnover, pricing can be hard. A house in Fordsville, Rockport or McHenry often has fewer nearby sales to compare against than one in Beaver Dam, so lean on recent closed sales and a good photo record of repairs.

Bills become payable on October 1, and the assessment date behind every bill is January 1. This is the calendar the sheriff follows.

Ohio County collection calendar
DatesAmount due
October 1 to November 1Bill less 2 percent
November 2 to December 31Face amount
January 1 to 31Face amount plus 5 percent
February 1 to April 15Face amount plus 21 percent
After April 15Bill transfers to the County Clerk

State law, in KRS 134.015, names a 10 percent charge for the late period, so ask the tax office to price your parcel exactly before you send a check.

If no bill has shown up by about October 10, call. The sheriff will send a duplicate by mail, fax or email. A copy sent to another address is a one-time courtesy, and only the PVA can change the standing mailing address.

sections.h2: What happens to bills left unpaid on April 15?
sections.html:
Prior-year payments leave the sheriff on April 15 and go to the Ohio County Clerk at 301 S Main St, Suite 201 in Hartford (weekdays 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.; recording desk 270-298-4423). The clerk's delinquent tax page lists the sale date, so call for the next one.

  • The bill becomes a recorded lien, and 1 percent interest is added each month.
  • Large-scale bidders (over three certificates here, five statewide or $10,000 in total) register with the state first.
  • A listed house with a certificate needs a written payoff from the clerk, since the balance grows each month.

Pay the balance before the sale if you can. Once an investor holds the certificate, you owe that investor, plus added fees.

Your first call goes to the PVA, 270-298-4433, and the required conference must take place while spring inspection is still open. Bring comparable sales, repair estimates and photos. If the conference fails, the next stops are a form at the County Clerk, then a local three-person board, then the state Board of Tax Appeals. The PVA appeal guide spells out each deadline, including 30 days to reach the state board.

Keep paying while you wait. An appeal that succeeds produces a refund, and the tax office handles those at the end of the month.

sections.h2: A year in the life of an Ohio County bill
sections.html:
It helps to see the whole cycle once. Value and ownership are fixed as of January 1. Statements arrive when bills become payable on October 1, and the early window closes November 1. The face amount holds until the end of December, then penalties begin in January and step up in February. By April 15 anything still owed has left the sheriff's hands.

For a seller, that rhythm decides who pays what. If you list in spring, you still owe the year's bill because you owned the house on January 1, and the buyer usually reimburses you for the months after closing. If you list in the fall, check whether the 2 percent discount is still open before the bill is paid. Whichever season you sell in, bring the most recent receipt to the closing agent along with the sheriff's phone number.

The homestead exemption is open to residents who are 65 or older or totally disabled. A 70 percent VA rating or a 100 percent Social Security disability finding can also qualify, and the PVA decides each claim. It takes a set dollar amount off the assessed value, revised on a two-year cycle, and the next owner starts a new application.

Working farmland is taxed on what the land earns from farming, not on market price. In a county where 76 percent of residents live in rural areas, that can matter a great deal, so ask the PVA about any tract you plan to sell or split.

sections.h2: What a seller owes besides the tax bill
sections.html:
The seller carries the state transfer tax: 50 cents per $500 of declared value, rounded up (KRS 142.050). It is due before the clerk accepts the deed.

  • Confirm with the sheriff who is paying this year's bill.
  • Ask the clerk about any recorded lien or certificate.
  • Put a tax-bill mailing address in the deed, as KRS 382.135 demands.

A sale that closes between January 1 and the next fall still leaves a bill in the seller's name, so write the split into the contract and keep the receipt.

sections.h2: Selling a house that has tax problems
sections.html:
Owing tax does not block a sale. The balance is paid out of your proceeds at closing, and the sheriff quotes it before April 15 while the County Clerk quotes it afterward. Here is the sequence.

  1. Call the right office and ask for a written payoff good through your closing date.
  2. Give the figure to the title company so it can pay the balance from your proceeds.
  3. Ask the clerk to confirm that any recorded lien has been released.
  4. Keep copies of the receipts for your files.

A cash sale skips the lender's appraisal and repair list, which helps with an older house, but the tax payoff still happens at the table. Self-employed owners and heirs with a vacant property should also check that nothing is recorded against the parcel before choosing a closing date.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Ohio County property tax?
faqs.a: The sheriff's tax office in Hartford, at 301 South Main Street. Mail checks to PO Box 186, Hartford, KY 42347.

faqs.q: When does a penalty begin on an Ohio County property tax bill?
faqs.a: On January 1. A 5 percent penalty covers that month, and any payment made from November 2 through the end of December costs just the face amount.

faqs.q: Can a house with an unpaid tax bill still be sold?
faqs.a: Yes. Payoff comes out of the proceeds, using a figure from the sheriff before April 15 or from the County Clerk after it.

faqs.q: Whom do I call to question my Ohio County valuation?
faqs.a: The PVA, 270-298-4433. Values are outside the sheriff's authority.

faqs.q: Who pays the transfer tax on an Ohio County sale?
faqs.a: The seller. It is 50 cents for each $500 of declared value, rounded up, and the clerk collects it before taking the deed.
